source: Sharma, Dumancic, King, Cropper (2025, v2 Jan 2026) Learning Logical Rules Using Minimum Message Length
finding: Head-to-head test of an MML cost against an MDL cost (C-MDL) for learning logic programs from noisy examples. Written by a Cambridge, Delft, Helsinki group, so not the Monash MML school. MML matched MDL on balanced and noisy data and beat it on small or lopsided data.
numbers: RandomLearner, 10 repeats, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected Wilcoxon tests, balanced accuracy. Q1a (30 tasks) and Q1b (10-50% noise, Alzheimer data): no significant difference. Q2 (train size 20 and 50): MML ahead in 12 of 12 size-proportion cells, significant (p<0.05) in 11. Q3: significant gain at all 8 sizes (1 to 500); more than 4% on 5 of 8; size 1 gives 6.8 +/- 2.4%. Q4: generality prior adds 6.6 +/- 2.6% at one example only, nothing at larger sizes. Q5 (ApproxLearner): positive-only data +9.2 +/- 2.7%, negative-only +25.9 +/- 4.0% (p<0.01).
limits: Authors say the MML prior may be too optimistic on noisy data. Datasets: Alzheimer, Zendo, 1D-ARC, Trains, but 1D-ARC numbers are not broken out in the results text I read. Compared with MDL only, not AIC or BIC. Logic programs, not LLM text.
agent_relevance: Best independent evidence that MML differs from MDL in practice: the gap shows up at 1 to 20 examples and in one-sided data. A scaffold that learns rules from very few cases may want a likelihood term that punishes over-general rules.

source: Sharma et al. (2026) mechanism section of the same paper
finding: Explains why MDL fails on positive-only data: the program that says everything is true has zero errors and is short, so MDL picks it. The MML likelihood charges a large cost for such a program, so MML prefers a program that covers only seen examples.
numbers: Cost of the all-true program under MML is large (log of all possible atoms over seen atoms); for a program covering only seen examples the term is log(1) = 0. C-MDL failed exactly at 100% positive examples.
limits: Author explanation backed by the Q2 and Q5 trend, not an ablation of the term itself.
agent_relevance: Same trap exists for an agent: a vague answer that fits every observation is cheap to state. Penalise generality that no observation could contradict.

source: Makalic and Schmidt (2022) Introduction to minimum message length inference
finding: Tutorial on MML. Strict MML has an exact polynomial algorithm only for one-dimensional discrete data (Farr and Wallace) and one-dimensional continuous exponential families (Dowty). For k-nomial with k>2 it is set partitioning and runs in exponential time. Rissanen's NML code length reduces to BIC as n grows.
numbers: Binomial n=10: strict MML partitions counts into {0}, {1..4}, {5..9}, {10} with estimates 0.00, 0.25, 0.70, 1.00. A naive partition costs about 9.84 bits, worse than the strict MML code.
limits: Tutorial by MML practitioners; invariance claims are asserted, not tested against rivals.
agent_relevance: Supports the NP-hard claim: an agent should use the Wallace-Freeman approximation, never strict MML.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC blog)
finding: Per-puzzle neural decoder trained by gradient descent to minimise total code length (reconstruction cross-entropy plus KL on a latent). The answer is the most frequent sample during training. Re-opened here: the earlier agent-reported figures are confirmed.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 pass@2 after 2000 iterations: train 34.75%, eval 20%. Eval peaked at 21.5% at 1500 iterations. At 1000 iterations: 31.75% / 19.25%. About 20 minutes per puzzle on an RTX 4070. No pretraining.
quote: A more efficient (i.e., lower-bit) compression of a puzzle correlates with a more accurate solution.
limits: Weight-regularisation term is omitted in the code, so it is not a full two-part code. Cannot do counting, rotation, reflection or long-range patterns. Latent can collapse and the run then fails. Blog, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A code-length signal works on ARC but costs about 20 minutes of training per puzzle, so it is not a cheap tie-break.

source: MADIL authors (2025) MADIL: MDL-based pattern decomposition for ARC
finding: An MDL-guided program learner for ARC with no LLM. It does well on ARC training tasks but poorly on private tasks and stays below LLM methods, as its abstract admits.
numbers: Abstract: 7% at ArcPrize 2024. Results table (text extraction partly scrambled): MADIL v3.5 shows 32.1% on training tasks and 6.0% on private tasks. Paper cites 30% at ARCathon 2023 and 55% at ArcPrize 2024 for LLM-heavy entries and says humans solve over 80%.
limits: I could not match every table cell to its column. Use only the abstract's 7% and the 32.1 / 6.0 pair.
agent_relevance: Shortest-description search alone does not generalise to unseen ARC tasks. Keep the shortest-rule rule as a tie-break, not the main solver.

source: Nair, Wang et al. (2024) MIDGARD: Self-Consistency Using Minimum Description Length
finding: Samples several reasoning graphs from an LLM and merges them with an MDL objective that charges different costs for adding and deleting an edge. Beats a single greedy generation on argument mining. This is MDL, not MML, and it merges graph parts rather than ranking whole answers.
numbers: Table 1, 5 seeds, macro average over ESSAYS/ABSTRCT/CDCP. gpt-3.5-turbo: component F1 greedy 68.5 vs MIDGARD 70.4; relation R100 23.7 vs 25.7; R50 34.7 vs 37.2. Code-Llama: 54.1 vs 55.6; R100 11.5 vs 16.5; R50 18.8 vs 24.9. Equal add and delete cost variant (lambda 0.5) scored 57.9 on component F1, below greedy 68.5. Spurious edges on ESSAYS 528.2 down to 469.0.
limits: Small gains, gpt-3.5 and Code-Llama only. Baseline is greedy decoding, so this is not a test against majority vote at equal tokens. Table cells partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to the answer-selection gap: an MDL merge adds about 2 points on gpt-3.5 and penalty design matters a lot. A design hint for the scaffold's merge step.

source: Gao, Das et al. (2026) RIMRULE: tool-using agents with MDL-consolidated rules
finding: The LLM proposes rules from failure traces; an MDL objective prunes and merges them into a small library injected into the prompt. Compression kept the rules useful.
numbers: MDL consolidation cut rule count 7% (ToolHop) and 20% (BFCL) and raised accuracy. Table 8 test-rand accuracy: prompt-based consolidation 27.5 +/- 1.4 (ToolHop), 52.1 +/- 0.9 (BFCL); MDL-guided 31.1 +/- 1.3 and 56.6 +/- 1.2. Low-resource run: 90 training samples, 4 rules, BFCL test-rand 55.2 to 62.1, test-unseen 46.0 to 60.0. Rules from Llama3.2 and GPT-4o transfer to other models including O1 and Llama4.
limits: Tool-use benchmarks only. The MDL score is the authors' own rules-length plus errors score; it is not MML.
agent_relevance: Direct support for compressing the scaffold's own memory when compression keeps explicit, tested rules (gap 8). Contrast with Lester et al., where blind compression hurt learnability.

source: Xu et al. (2026) ReuseRL: agentic RL with an MDL skill dictionary
finding: Adds a segmentation cost (skill dictionary code length) to GRPO. Plain shortest-trajectory pressure can backfire, while structural compression helps.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Qwen3-1.7B on TextWorld-Cooking), 300 GRPO steps. Pure round-length penalty fell 10.94 points below vanilla GRPO on TW-Cooking. Segmentation cost beat pure length by +0.71 / +1.49 (ALFWorld IID / OOD), +17.70 (TW-Cooking), +3.35 (Countdown). Greedy BPE dictionary within 0.14% of brute force, recovers 99.02% of phrases; exact optimum is NP-hard.
limits: Small models; training-time reward, not an inference scaffold. ALFWorld uses SC@7 majority vote, others pass@1 over 3 runs.
agent_relevance: Warning for any length-based tie-break: shortest is not always best. Reward structure that recurs across successes, not raw brevity.

source: Donoway, Joren, Roger, Leike (2026) Excess Description Length of Learning Generalizable Predictors
finding: Builds Excess Description Length (EDL) from prequential coding: bits to code training labels with the evolving model minus bits under the final model. It avoids coding the model but depends on data order. Used to tell elicitation from teaching in fine-tuning.
numbers: EDL is about zero for random labels; one example can remove up to log m bits about which of m hypotheses holds; a threshold near 1+ bits per trainable parameter separates teaching from elicitation.
limits: Fine-tuning with labels, not reasoning traces. No test of prequential versus two-part scoring on chain-of-thought correctness.
agent_relevance: A formal prequential tool exists, but gap 2 (do earlier steps predict later ones in correct reasoning) is still unmeasured by anyone I found.

source: Pan, Wang, Liao, Li (2025) Understanding LLM Behaviors via Compression
finding: Treats LLM training as two-part coding under the Kolmogorov structure function and builds a Syntax-Knowledge data model to explain scaling laws, knowledge acquisition and hallucination.
numbers: Text search: zero occurrences of 'message length'. Experiments said to validate the theory; numbers not extracted.
limits: Theory-led. Uses Kolmogorov two-part language, not MML.
agent_relevance: A 2025 case of the two-part lineage used without naming MML (gap 9).

source: Huang, Zuk, Magauin, Huang, Liu (2026) Structure-Residual Inductive Biases for LM Pretraining
finding: Uses a structure plus residual two-part view to design two training modules. No MML cited.
numbers: GPT-2 Medium, 300M tokens: combined NLL gain 1.44%, persists to 20B tokens. Zero occurrences of 'message length'.
limits: Pretraining method, not a thinking scaffold.
agent_relevance: More evidence for gap 9: two-part ideas appear in 2026 LLM work, not under the MML name.

source: Spangher, Ho, Yang, Goodman, Koyejo (2026) Articulation Upper Bounds for Language Models
finding: A near-name hit that is not MML. Message length there means prompt word count. Appendix D.2 states neither measure uses message length, and a search summary reports median message length does not track recovery.
numbers: 1.2k concepts, eight domains. Prompt optimiser beats existing ones by up to 14% (abstract).
limits: The message-length versus recovery claim is from Table 6 headings and the search summary; I did not read the full table.
agent_relevance: Short messages are not automatically better transmitted. Another caution against brevity-only scoring.

source: Wallace and Boulton (1968) An information measure for classification, Computer Journal 11(2)
finding: Only the abstract page was readable; full text is paywalled. Abstract: classification as economical statistical encoding of attribute information; program SNOB on the Sydney KDF 9; first tests show good agreement with conventional taxonomy.
numbers: No data, class counts or bit thresholds available from the page.
limits: Gap 5 (10-bit thresholds, class counts) cannot be answered from open sources.
agent_relevance: Cannot reuse Snob thresholds as a stop rule; use a generic rule (accept a new part only if it shortens the total message).

source: Bartlett, Desmond, Ferreira (2023) Priors for Symbolic Regression
finding: Compares Bayesian, MDL and heuristic selection of equations with language-model priors. Cites Wallace and Freeman 1987 but does not run MML. MDL beat the Bayesian method on Korns-1 and Korns-6 per the text read.
numbers: Partial read; exact tables not extracted.
limits: Not an MML head-to-head; MDL versus Bayesian only.
agent_relevance: A model-selection example with a language-model prior, not MML evidence.
